result.improved: The plant can stabilize and slowly recover lost reserves.
result.stabilized: Acute pressure was contained, but still matters in the background.
result.worsened: Stress remained active and kept weighing on growth or stability.
result.escalated: Pressure developed into a clearer follow-up problem.
result.unresolved: The plant remains vulnerable for now, even without hard escalation.

guidance.improved: Keep the correction steady and watch for stable values.
guidance.stabilized: The situation is contained, but still needs one to two clean follow-up cycles.
guidance.worsened: Pressure is not resolved yet. Small targeted corrections beat rushed reactions.
guidance.escalated: The situation keeps escalating. Prioritize containment over growth pushes.
guidance.unresolved: Watch the next cycles and only correct the real trigger.

problem_source.water_wet: The medium stayed wet too long, reducing oxygen in the root zone.
problem_source.water_dry: The root ball dried out too far and the plant had to compensate for water stress.
problem_source.nutrition_lockout: Uptake was unstable. EC or pH drift shifted nutrient availability.
problem_source.nutrition_deficit: The current nutrient buffer no longer matched this growth phase.
problem_source.disease_mold: Humidity, low airflow, or dense canopy pushed the microclimate out of balance.
problem_source.environment_heat_dry: Heat and dry airflow increased transpiration pressure.
problem_source.environment_cold: Temperatures dropped too far and slowed metabolism and water uptake.
problem_source.environment_light: Light intensity and canopy distance were too aggressive for the current condition.
problem_source.generic: Multiple stressors built up over time and created the current pressure.

indoor_dry_rootball.title: Dry rootball with uneven moisture recovery
indoor_dry_rootball.symptom: The surface looks dry, leaf tension drops, and water runs unevenly. The core lacks moisture while edge zones react faster than the rest of the pot.
indoor_dry_rootball.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Rehydrate in small steps instead of flooding. This gives the dry core time to reconnect with moisture without overloading the pot.
coach.why: When the rootball core dries out, water often bypasses it along the sides. Split watering restores contact in the substrate and lowers the risk of symptom-only fixes.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: After a calm rehydration, moisture spreads more evenly again. Leaf tension improves, pot behavior becomes predictable, and panic rewatering is less likely.

indoor_heat_stress_air.title: Heat load above the canopy
indoor_heat_stress_air.symptom: Leaf edges curl slightly and the canopy looks tense. Warm air and dry flow pull more water from the leaf than roots can calmly replace.
indoor_heat_stress_air.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Cool the air and canopy zone first instead of watering on reflex. Temperature, airflow, and light load need to work together again.
coach.why: The stress sits in the air and leaf surface, not automatically in the pot. When the canopy runs too hot, transpiration outruns supply.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: Once the heat peak drops, leaf posture often relaxes quickly. Water demand and follow-up corrections become easier to read again.

lower_canopy_temp.detail: Cuts direct load from the canopy and relieves the plant faster than another watering reflex.

increase_air_exchange.detail: Helps dump warm air as long as the airflow does not turn even drier and harsher.

raise_light_intensity.detail: More light raises load on an already hot canopy and pushes the diagnosis the wrong way.

indoor_light_nutrient_tox_early.title: Early nutrient stress from light and feed load
indoor_light_nutrient_tox_early.symptom: Leaf tips show first overload signs. Light pressure and feed strength are out of balance, pushing the plant into avoidable stress early in the cycle.
indoor_light_nutrient_tox_early.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Lower pressure briefly and recalibrate light and feed in small steps. This restores uptake stability without harsh counter-moves.
coach.why: When light intensity and nutrient strength do not match, metabolic pressure rises faster than the plant can process. Small corrections work better than extreme reversals.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: After a gentle correction, new growth usually settles quickly. Efficiency improves and the next adjustment becomes much clearer.

indoor_overwatering_early.title: Early overwatering in the root zone
indoor_overwatering_early.symptom: Leaves hang softly while the pot is still heavy. The root zone stays too wet and gets too little air, so uptake slows down even though enough water is present.
indoor_overwatering_early.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Do not water again yet. Bring air back into the root zone, stabilize the rhythm, and watch the trend before your next correction.
coach.why: In early overwatering, the core issue is often oxygen shortage in the substrate, not missing water. If the pot stays wet too long, roots respond slowly and thirst-like signals still appear.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: With a short watering pause and better airflow, root stress usually drops. New leaves recover a steadier posture and your watering rhythm becomes easier to.

indoor_soil_ph_out_of_range.title: pH is slowing nutrient uptake
indoor_soil_ph_out_of_range.symptom: Leaves look deficient even though nutrients are still in the medium. pH has drifted away from target and is blocking part of the uptake.
indoor_soil_ph_out_of_range.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Measure pH first and correct it in small steps. More feed helps little if the plant cannot take it up well right now.
coach.why: pH is not just a lab number. It helps decide which nutrients stay available at the root zone.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: Once pH returns to range, follow-up corrections work better. New growth looks calmer and the trend is easier to read.

adjust_ph_gradual.detail: Targets the cause directly and eases uptake without a hard swing.

verify_runoff_then_adjust.detail: Confirms the reading first so you do not push pH the wrong way.

add_more_nutrients_now.detail: More feed without measurement often raises pressure while uptake stays blocked.

indoor_vpd_mismatch_veg.title: Climate is off for early veg
indoor_vpd_mismatch_veg.symptom: Leaves look slack one moment and tense the next, even with decent watering and feed. Temperature and humidity are not pulling together.
indoor_vpd_mismatch_veg.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Stabilize climate first instead of chasing the issue with water or feed. Veg growth needs a calm range for transpiration and uptake.
coach.why: VPD describes how hard the air pulls water from the leaf. When it swings too high or too low, temperature, humidity, and transpiration stop working together.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: With calmer climate, the plant works more evenly again. Leaf tension and growth are easier to read.

rebalance_temp_humidity.detail: Brings temperature and humidity back into a calmer working range.

stabilize_then_monitor.detail: Prevents overreaction and shows whether one small climate change is already enough.

chase_with_random_changes.detail: Too many quick climate changes blur the cause and often push stress higher.

outdoor_cold_night_stress.title: Cold nights visibly slow plant metabolism
outdoor_cold_night_stress.symptom: After cold nights, morning growth response looks sluggish and slightly droopy. Uptake slows down while daytime demand rises again, creating an unstable daily pattern.
outdoor_cold_night_stress.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Buffer night conditions and avoid rushed morning overreactions. Give the plant time to return to a stable temperature flow.
coach.why: Low night temperature reduces enzyme activity and root speed. If daytime pressure rises too fast, demand and root delivery fall out of sync.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: With better night buffering, the daily start becomes smoother. The plant reacts less abruptly and climate-care tuning gets easier.

outdoor_heatwave_dry_wind.title: Heatwave plus dry wind
outdoor_heatwave_dry_wind.symptom: Leaves lose tension even when some moisture may still be in the pot. Heat and dry wind pull water from the leaf faster than roots can replace it.
outdoor_heatwave_dry_wind.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Take load off the spot before pouring in more water. Shade, wind cover, and calmer timing help more here than panic push.
coach.why: Hot air and dry wind raise transpiration together. The balance between leaf demand and root supply can break fast even while some water remains in the pot.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: With shade and calmer airflow, leaf tension usually returns step by step. Water timing and follow-up moves become clearer.

shade_and_windbreak.detail: Cuts direct load from sun and airflow without rebuilding the whole outdoor setup.

water_timing_adjust_dawn.detail: Builds reserve before the hottest part of the day, but works best with site relief.

defoliate_midday.detail: Removes leaf area right inside the stress peak and slows recovery.

outdoor_heavy_rain_waterlogging_risk.title: Heavy rain raises waterlogging risk in pots
outdoor_heavy_rain_waterlogging_risk.symptom: After strong rain, pots stay heavy and leaves lose tension. The root zone remains saturated too long, reducing oxygen and slowing uptake despite high moisture.
outdoor_heavy_rain_waterlogging_risk.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Prioritize drainage now and allow a dry window. Adding more water would be counterproductive because roots need air and structure first.
coach.why: During prolonged saturation, pore space fills with water instead of air. Root function drops and stress signals appear even though water is not lacking.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: With better drainage and patience, root pressure drops. Plants often recover posture and the risk of follow-up stress stays manageable.

shared_early_pest_signs_mild.title: Early pest traces
shared_early_pest_signs_mild.symptom: Fine traces are showing on leaf undersides and a few small spots. It is still mild, which makes this the best moment for calm control.
shared_early_pest_signs_mild.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Inspect carefully and stay calm instead of treating everything at once. Early signs reward observation, clean control, and small steps.
coach.why: Mild pest signs are not a panic alarm, but they are a strong diagnosis window. Reading undersides and patterns early saves the plant later blanket treatment.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: Early control usually keeps pressure small. You keep the overview and need harsh follow-up treatment less often.

targeted_inspection_isolation.detail: Checks hotspots directly and keeps the response small before spread grows.

increase_monitoring_frequency.detail: Tightens checks for a few days and quickly shows whether pressure is really rising.

spray_everything_blindly.detail: Broad spraying without a target stresses the plant and blurs your diagnosis.

shared_light_distance_error.title: Light distance error with avoidable stress
shared_light_distance_error.symptom: Early stress signals appear because distance to the light source is off. Too close or too far reduces efficiency and can amplify side stress in other systems.
shared_light_distance_error.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Adjust distance in small controlled steps. This stabilizes light load without triggering new stress peaks from oversized corrections.
coach.why: Large distance jumps change load abruptly and make plant responses harder to read. Gradual adjustments keep cause and effect clearer.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: With cleaner distance tuning, leaf behavior calms down. Light use improves and follow-up issues in water or climate appear less often.

shared_rootbound_warning.title: Root space is getting too tight
shared_rootbound_warning.symptom: The pot dries at the edge first but stays heavy inside. Roots have little room left, so uptake and growth respond more slowly.
shared_rootbound_warning.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.

coach.summary: Check the pot now instead of only adding more water. When root space is full, a planned transition helps more than extra rescue feeding.
coach.why: In a rootbound pot, roots circle the wall, water spreads unevenly, and the plant reacts more slowly even with decent care. Earlier action is easier than late rescue.

actions.0: Measure and observe first, then correct.
actions.1: Apply only one change per cycle.

aftermath.lesson: With more root space, moisture evens out again. Uptake and growth calm down, and you spend less time chasing symptoms.

plan_repot_next_window.detail: Sets up the next larger pot in time and relieves the crowded root zone cleanly.

optimize_watering_until_repot.detail: Keeps the plant steadier until the repot, but does not solve the space limit itself.

force_heavy_feed_now.detail: More feed does not fix a space problem and can raise pressure inside the full pot.

lc_climate_vpd_basics.title: Climate & VPD basics
lc_climate_vpd_basics.subtitle: Think temperature and humidity together

bullets.1: Small climate corrections are usually more stable.
bullets.2: Check leaf posture after each change.

lc_climate_vpd_basics.real_world_note: Good climate is a balance of temperature, RH, and airflow.

lc_ph_nutrient_uptake_basics.title: pH & nutrient uptake
lc_ph_nutrient_uptake_basics.subtitle: Not only what you feed, but what is absorbed

bullets.1: More fertilizer does not solve uptake lockouts.
bullets.2: Correct in small steps and read trends.

lc_ph_nutrient_uptake_basics.real_world_note: Uptake issues often look like deficiency.

lc_watering_basics.title: Read watering correctly
lc_watering_basics.subtitle: Water by signal, not by panic

bullets.0: Pot weight is a strong indicator.
bullets.1: Wet soil plus droop can mean overwatering.
bullets.2: Slow rehydration is usually more stable.

lc_watering_basics.real_world_note: Root-zone oxygen is key for stable uptake.

lc_rootzone_oxygen_basics.title: Roots need air
lc_rootzone_oxygen_basics.subtitle: Why wet dense medium can stress a plant anyway

bullets.0: Roots work best when enough oxygen is still available in the medium.
bullets.1: If substrate stays wet or dense, gas exchange drops and stress rises quickly.
bullets.2: Dryback, structure, and drainage are all part of watering practice.

lc_rootzone_oxygen_basics.real_world_note: A wet heavy pot can look well supplied while the root zone is actually running short on air.

lc_airflow_fundamentals.title: Airflow shapes climate
lc_airflow_fundamentals.subtitle: Gentle movement helps, hard wind stresses

bullets.0: Gentle airflow moves moisture away and breaks up warm pockets in the canopy.
bullets.1: Good airflow supports transpiration and stronger stems, but it is not hard wind.
bullets.2: Solve stale air and harsh exposure separately: air path indoors, shelter outdoors.

lc_airflow_fundamentals.real_world_note: The right amount of air movement feels stable, not aggressive. Plants should be able to breathe, not fight all day.

lc_light_intensity_distance_basics.title: Read light distance calmly
lc_light_intensity_distance_basics.subtitle: Think intensity, distance, and leaf signal together

bullets.0: Bright tops often mean the canopy is getting too much direct light.
bullets.1: Raise distance or lower intensity step by step instead of reacting hard.
bullets.2: Pale upper leaves do not automatically mean a nutrient problem.

lc_light_intensity_distance_basics.real_world_note: Light stress is usually corrected at the setup. More feed rarely fixes bleached tops.

lc_pest_observation_basics.title: Read early pest signs
lc_pest_observation_basics.subtitle: Check leaf undersides, monitor, then act with intent

bullets.0: Mild specks or eggs often show up under leaves first.
bullets.1: Early monitoring is usually stronger than late panic treatment.
bullets.2: Targeted inspection helps more than spraying everything blindly.

lc_pest_observation_basics.real_world_note: Pests found early can usually be slowed down with calmer, cleaner decisions.

lc_training_recovery_basics.title: Training needs recovery
lc_training_recovery_basics.subtitle: Stress stacks faster than a plant can bounce back

bullets.0: Bending, pruning, and reshaping all cost recovery energy.
bullets.1: Stacked interventions often slow new growth more than expected.
bullets.2: Stabilize first, read the response, then decide on the next step.

lc_training_recovery_basics.real_world_note: Strong training routines include quiet windows where the plant can rebuild tension and rhythm.

lc_recovery_observation_basics.title: Observe recovery first
lc_recovery_observation_basics.subtitle: Sometimes waiting is the next smart care move

bullets.0: If posture and tension are returning, you may not need another correction yet.
bullets.1: After a good fix, observation often helps more than a second reaction.
bullets.2: Recovery becomes clearer when you give the plant a little time.

lc_recovery_observation_basics.real_world_note: Plants often improve with a delay. Correcting again too early can interrupt that recovery.

indoor_fan_failure_airflow_drop.title: Airflow drops out
indoor_fan_failure_airflow_drop.symptom: Air feels still and heavy around the top of the canopy.
indoor_fan_failure_airflow_drop.description: Air movement is too weak or has dropped away. Warm humid pockets stay between the leaves and the room stops breathing well around the plant.
indoor_fan_failure_airflow_drop.cause: Without gentle air movement, leaf moisture dries off more slowly. That raises microclimate stress and makes weak tissue more likely.

coach.summary: This is not a feed issue. Restore the air path through the canopy first.
actions: Bring airflow back to plant height and break up dead zones in the canopy.
After the fix, watch humidity and leaf response calmly for a few hours.
coach.why: Airflow moves moisture away, supports transpiration, and keeps warm humid pockets from sitting right on the leaves.

aftermath.lesson: Airflow is part of the plant climate. Too little movement can stress a plant even before temperatures look extreme.

indoor_light_burn_canopy_top.title: Light sits too close to the top
indoor_light_burn_canopy_top.symptom: Upper leaves, edges, or tips start paling while the rest still looks calm. That points more to excess light at the top than to missing feed.
indoor_light_burn_canopy_top.description: The plant shows early signs of a manageable problem.
indoor_light_burn_canopy_top.cause: The uppermost zone is taking more light or heat than it can buffer right now. The reaction sits at the top, not evenly through the whole plant.

coach.summary: Check distance or intensity before feeding harder. Small light corrections are cleaner here than a reflex on nutrients.
actions: Raise the lamp a little or lower intensity in a moderate step.
Mark the affected tips and compare only the new growth after 24 hours.
coach.why: When only the top zone brightens, the cause often sits in light load. More nutrients do not fix overwhelmed leaf tips.

aftermath.lesson: With better distance, the top settles down again. New tips come in more evenly and light stress is easier to separate from real deficiency signals.

adjust_light_distance_stepwise.detail: Lowers light load in a controlled way and gives you a cleaner read on recovery.

measure_then_wait_24h.detail: Prevents overcorrection and makes the next response from the top easier to read.

feed_more_for_pale_top.detail: Extra feed confuses light stress with deficiency and hides the real cause.

indoor_rootzone_airless_medium.title: Root zone runs out of air
indoor_rootzone_airless_medium.symptom: The medium stays dense, heavy, and cool for too long.
indoor_rootzone_airless_medium.description: The root zone is too wet or too compact. Water is present, but gas exchange in the medium is too weak and the roots start responding slowly.
indoor_rootzone_airless_medium.cause: Roots need oxygen. When pore space stays filled with water, root respiration drops and stress rises even though the pot looks fully supplied.

coach.summary: This needs air more than water. Restore a dryback window and better structure first.
actions: Wait before the next watering so the root zone can breathe again.
Loosen the surface or improve the drainage path without panic-repotting the plant.
coach.why: A wet dense root zone blocks water movement and gas exchange at the same time. To the plant that feels like a poorly functioning root system.

aftermath.lesson: Water only helps when the root zone can still breathe.

outdoor_pot_dries_by_afternoon.title: Outdoor pot crashes by afternoon
outdoor_pot_dries_by_afternoon.symptom: The plant dips in the warm half of the day even though morning moisture looked decent. Sun, wind, and limited pot volume drain the reserve faster than expected.
outdoor_pot_dries_by_afternoon.description: Outdoors, the pot loses water through sun, wind, and small volume faster than the morning can buffer. The pattern is rhythmic more than permanent.
outdoor_pot_dries_by_afternoon.cause: A small or exposed pot drops into deficit faster through the day. This is often timing and volume, not instant proof of bad care overall.

coach.summary: Stabilize timing and site instead of pouring in more water during the heat. Water timing, light cover, and pot volume matter more here than panic.
actions: Move watering earlier so the pot enters the hot part of the day with reserve.
Use mulch, light cover, or more volume to soften the evaporation peak.
coach.why: With outdoor pots, the issue is not only how much water goes in, but when it goes in and how fast it leaves again. Chasing the midday drop often only treats the symptom.

aftermath.lesson: When timing and site fit better, the plant stays steadier through the day. Then it becomes clearer whether later mulch or more volume is really needed.

water_timing_adjust_dawn.detail: Builds reserve before the heat and supports the harder second half of the day more cleanly.

shade_and_windbreak.detail: Lowers evaporative pressure through site relief when sun and wind are pulling together.

double_feed_in_heat.detail: More feed does not replace missing water and can make the dry daytime stress harsher.

outdoor_early_pest_pressure_leaf_undersi.title: Early pest pressure under leaves
outdoor_early_pest_pressure_leaf_undersi.symptom: Mild specks or traces show up on leaf undersides.
outdoor_early_pest_pressure_leaf_undersi.description: The damage is still light, but it already sits where people often look too rarely. Outside, that early signal can disappear into the routine very quickly.
outdoor_early_pest_pressure_leaf_undersi.cause: Early pressure often begins small: a few specks, faint traces, first activity under protected leaf surfaces. The key move right now is observation, not panic action.

coach.summary: Not a panic case yet. Check cleanly and respond with precision.
actions: Inspect undersides carefully and keep the affected areas on a short watch.
Reduce pressure mechanically or with a narrow response instead of blanket treatment.
coach.why: The earlier the pattern is identified, the smaller the intervention can stay. Overreaction often stresses the plant more than the first signal did.

aftermath.lesson: Early pest signals are usually small. The difference comes from calm follow-up and better looking.

outdoor_wind_exposure_stem_stress.title: Wind stresses stems and shoots
outdoor_wind_exposure_stem_stress.symptom: Shoots lean hard and begin to show rub or pressure marks.
outdoor_wind_exposure_stem_stress.description: The site is too exposed or the plant was moved into stronger airflow too quickly. The stimulus is no longer gentle movement but constant mechanical load.
outdoor_wind_exposure_stem_stress.cause: Light movement strengthens tissue, but steady gusts or abrupt exposure cost stability and water. Young plants can slide into stress fast under that load.

coach.summary: Stabilize first and harden off more slowly.
actions: Support the shoots or reduce sway until the plant stands cleanly again.
Use shelter and build new exposure only step by step.
coach.why: Hardening off means measured exposure. Too much wind at once drains water and strains tissue instead of building resilience.

aftermath.lesson: Air movement helps, but constant drag is not training. Outdoor exposure has to be built.

shared_panic_watering_misread.title: Droop is not a watering answer yet
shared_panic_watering_misread.symptom: Leaves hang, but that can mean too wet or too dry. Without pot weight, timing, and substrate feel, the water picture is still open.
shared_panic_watering_misread.description: Drooping leaves quickly trigger the reflex to water again. That is the trap: the same picture can mean too wet, too dry, or simply time-of-day pressure.
shared_panic_watering_misread.cause: If you react only to leaf posture, you skip the real diagnosis. Weight, substrate feel, and timing tell you whether water is missing or already too much is there.

coach.summary: Check the pot first, then act. One short check saves you from covering an unclear signal with even more water.
actions: Check real pot weight or moisture before adding new water.
If the picture stays unclear, wait briefly and factor in root zone plus time of day.
coach.why: The same droop signal can come from opposite causes. Good care separates observation from reaction instead of mixing both in one panic move.

aftermath.lesson: When you read first and water second, droop signals become useful again. That is how you learn the difference between real thirst and wet-root stress.

check_weight_before_watering.detail: Separates instinct from diagnosis and gives you a better chance to choose correctly.

inspect_rootzone_then_wait.detail: Helps with mixed signals when you still need to judge whether wetness or dryness is leading.

water_on_panic_signal.detail: Can push an already wet root zone further and make the signal even harder to read afterward.

shared_substrate_drainage_compaction.title: Drainage is collapsing in the mix
shared_substrate_drainage_compaction.symptom: Water enters slowly and the surface starts sealing over. Lower in the pot, the root zone stays wet long after the top already invites another move.
shared_substrate_drainage_compaction.description: The substrate is losing structure. Water stands longer, air pores disappear, and the root-zone rhythm becomes sluggish.
shared_substrate_drainage_compaction.cause: Compacted or weak-draining medium slows runoff and gas exchange at the same time. It looks like a watering mistake, but the real problem sits in the substrate build.

coach.summary: Fix structure and runoff first instead of only watering more or less. The problem sits in the medium, not only in the volume.
actions: Improve drainage at the surface and along the runoff path.
Plan a repot or substrate correction at the next sensible window.
coach.why: When air pores collapse, water moves poorly and oxygen moves in poorly. That is why every watering cycle starts to feel messy.

aftermath.lesson: With looser structure, the root zone runs calmer. Water drains more predictably and you spend less time correcting swampy spots or dry pockets.

improve_drainage_surface.detail: Reopens the upper choke point and helps water plus air move through the medium more cleanly.

plan_repot_next_window.detail: Makes sense if compaction sits deeper and a later clean reset helps more than patching.

keep_watering_same_volume.detail: Keeps the same pattern alive and only pushes a structure problem into the next cycle.

indoor_overtraining_stall_mild.title: Training got stacked too fast
indoor_overtraining_stall_mild.symptom: Fresh growth stalls after several interventions in a short window.
indoor_overtraining_stall_mild.description: The plant has taken too many training signals without enough recovery space. Instead of building forward, it shifts energy into stress handling and repair.
indoor_overtraining_stall_mild.cause: Every bend, cut, and correction needs recovery time. When those actions stack, the plant loses the clean pause it needs to answer well.

coach.summary: No more shaping right now. Give stability and quiet back first.
actions: Pause all training for a few days and observe instead of correcting again.
Keep climate steady so the plant can spend energy on recovery instead of defense.
coach.why: More intervention will not fix the stall. Wait until tension and fresh growth return before you touch structure again.

aftermath.lesson: Recovery is part of training. Good structure comes from rhythm, not nonstop intervention.

shared_observation_recovery_after_stress.title: Recovery becomes visible
shared_observation_recovery_after_stress.symptom: The plant is lifting again and looks noticeably calmer.
shared_observation_recovery_after_stress.description: After a clean correction, the plant starts to show clear recovery signs. This is the moment where observation is worth more than one more action.
shared_observation_recovery_after_stress.cause: The last correction worked and the plant is regulating for itself again. Jumping in too quickly often interrupts that rebound.

coach.summary: It is coming back. Watch now and do not stack new actions.
actions: Observe calmly for 24 hours and do not interrupt the rebound with another correction.
Read leaf tension and fresh growth speed before reaching for water again.
coach.why: Recovery teaches as much as stress does. If you learn to read this phase, later decisions get calmer and cleaner.

aftermath.lesson: Improvement is a signal too. Not every positive shift needs an immediate follow-up action.

watering_rootzone_chain.title: From misread watering to air-starved roots
watering_rootzone_chain.summary: This chain links misread thirst signals, fast outdoor dryback, weak drainage, and oxygen-poor medium into one clear watering-to-root-zone story.

airflow_climate_chain.title: From airflow loss to climate stress
airflow_climate_chain.summary: This chain starts with stale indoor air, escalates through VPD and heat pressure, and uses the outdoor branch to show how exposure and dry wind extend the same microclimate problem.
